comparison: Both strongly support the AI-based virtual screening workflow and compound identification (C6, C33-C37, C96-C99). OpenEval emphasizes the methodological details and hit rate, while peer reviewers highlight this as a main strength with 'comprehensive and clear' experimental validation. Peer review also includes C38-C39 (trafficking validation) which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

Both strongly support the pharmacochaperone activity and trafficking rescue data (C7, C40-C43). OpenEval notes the dose-response quantification and use of multiple mutants. Peer reviewers describe the data as 'comprehensive and clear, with very convincing cell biological and patch-clamp data.' Both evaluations are fully aligned with no concerns raised.

Perfect agreement on reversibility findings (C8, C44-C45, C48). Both evaluations emphasize the reversible inhibition as a key distinguishing feature from high-affinity inhibitors. OpenEval highlights the complementary assay methods, while peer reviewers note this can be 'readily washed off' as a main strength. Complete concordance on this critical finding.

Strong agreement on functional recovery after washout (C9, C49-C51). Both recognize this as the key therapeutic advantage over existing pharmacochaperones. OpenEval notes the comparison with GBC and diazoxide response data. Peer reviewers emphasize this enables 'function of rescued channels' which is 'important for therapeutic application.' Both fully support these claims.

Both support the selectivity data (C52-C54, C75) showing ~4-5 fold preference for SUR1 over SUR2. OpenEval notes the modest but potentially sufficient selectivity. Peer reviewers accept the data as 'well-conceived and executed' and relevant to therapeutic application, though both acknowledge cardiovascular effects need further evaluation.

Both support the cryoEM structure determination (C10, C55-C58). OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of the 4.1Å resolution and structure workflow. Peer reviewers describe the structural analysis as 'comprehensive and clear' from 'leading experts.' Peer review R5 also encompasses detailed binding interactions (C59-C65) which OpenEval addresses separately in R8.

Both support the detailed molecular interactions from the structure (C59-C65). OpenEval notes the resolution is marginal for some specific interactions and acknowledges weaker density for the imidazole group. Peer reviewers accept the structural characterization without criticism, describing experiments as 'well-conceived and executed.'

Perfect agreement on MD simulation data (C66-C67). Both support the conformational analysis showing flexibility of the imidazole group. OpenEval provides technical details on simulation time and equilibration. Peer reviewers treat the simulations as part of comprehensive structural characterization without raising concerns.

Strong agreement on mutagenesis validation (C68-C72). Both evaluations support the functional validation of the structural model through systematic mutagenesis. OpenEval notes internal consistency and appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse 'functional validation of several residues involved in drug sensitivity' as well-executed. Peer review also includes C80 (site A classification) which OpenEval addresses in R13.

Both express uncertainty about therapeutic promise and AI claims (C73-C74, C78). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are conclusions requiring extensive additional validation. Peer reviewers are mixed: they question advantages over existing compounds and raise concerns about cardiovascular effects, but recognize conceptual advance and potential. Both acknowledge the challenging path to clinical application.

Strong agreement on study limitations and future work needed (C76-C77, C93-C95). OpenEval supports these as appropriate acknowledgments of what additional work is required. Peer reviewers explicitly raise concerns about cardiovascular effects and in vivo applicability that the authors acknowledge. Both parties recognize extensive validation is needed before clinical translation.

OpenEval supports conservation of effects in human channels (C46-C47) based on sequence homology, noting more extensive characterization would strengthen conclusions. Peer review R2 includes C46 as part of the trafficking rescue data and accepts it without specific comment on the human channel validation.

Both support the classification of Aekatperone as a site A ligand (C80). OpenEval provides context relating to established binding models and notes that site occupancy doesn't determine affinity/reversibility. Peer review includes C80 as part of the mutagenesis validation without specific discussion of the site A/B classification framework.
